title: Theatre attire, gloves, footwear and jewellery
audience: Operating-theatre staff, scrubbed and non-scrubbed, and visitors who enter the main theatre. Cleaning contractors apply the cleaning and waste steps only; surgical technique is for theatre clinicians.
learningOutcomes: Choose and use gloves, including double gloving for high-risk procedures, under the theatre plan.
State the rules for headwear, footwear, jewellery and nails in the theatre.
Describe which items come off before someone exits the theatre.

instruction.heading: Gloves have two jobs
instruction.body: Gloves guard the person wearing them against the patient blood and wound exudate, and they also stop organisms on the wearer hands from reaching the surgical site. The theatre document says double gloving reduces hand contamination and protects the wearer against viral transmission, and it recommends double gloving for high-risk procedures. The learner guide adds that gloves are single-use, never washed for reuse, replaced when damaged, and that hands are cleaned before and after putting them on. Where the two sources cover the same point, the learner guide governs.

instruction.heading: Gowns, masks and eye shields
instruction.body: Scrubbed staff face the greatest splash risk. The theatre document recommends fluid-resistant face masks, which give both an airborne barrier and splash protection. For heavy contamination it advises gowns that are impermeable, with waterproof sleeves that reach well down the arm and a front panel covering the full length of the body; for scrubbed staff losing a lot of fluid it suggests plastic aprons; and for the eyes it names goggles or a face shield that covers the whole face. Everyone who wears protective items is trained in their fit and use, and the equipment is checked, maintained and restocked so that it is always available.

instruction.heading: Headwear
instruction.body: Disposable headwear is required for scrubbed staff, since they stand near the surgical field, which matters most in laminar flow rooms. Hats are also needed in laminar flow rooms when a prosthesis is being implanted. Headwear is discarded after use and is never worn outside the theatre.

instruction.heading: Footwear
instruction.body: Footwear should fit well and have impervious soles. Open footwear is not worn. Protective boots, such as galoshes or rubber boots reaching the calf, are the better choice over standard shoes. Shoes are wiped down each time they are worn, and a set routine at the close of each session makes sure that happens. The learner guide asks for footwear that protects against dropped sharps, which fits with this.

instruction.heading: Jewellery and nails
instruction.body: Chains, earrings and gem-set rings are removed. Plain bands can remain on for both scrubbed and unscrubbed staff, but surgeons may be asked to take them off, mainly when metal implants are in use. The learner guide allows only a plain flat band, and only where the organisation permits it, so the theatre policy decides. False fingernails are not worn in the theatre.

instruction.heading: Visitors and leaving the theatre
instruction.body: A visitor entering a main theatre changes into theatre clothing first. Scrubbed staff wear disposable caps, masks and footwear close to the field. Before exiting, take the surgical mask off (never let it hang on the neck), remove the cap, and put a fresh white jacket over the theatre clothes whenever you leave the unit, particularly when walking through public corridors.

procedure: Check the theatre plan for the case and confirm which protective items apply.
Check each pair of gloves for size and damage before use, and double glove where the plan requires it.
Put on headwear, mask and eye protection at the point the plan sets, and check the fit.
If a glove tears, remove it, wash the hands, and put on a new glove before continuing (see “Sharps and instruments in theatre”).
Before leaving the theatre, remove the mask and the cap, and put on the white jacket if you are leaving the department.
Wash reusable footwear and put it away at the close of each session.

workedExamples.situation: During a high-risk case, a scrubbed nurse glove tears.
workedExamples.reasoning: Remove the torn glove, wash the hands with the scrub solution, and put on a new glove. Check that no sharp or instrument involved is still in the sterile field, and follow the steps in “Sharps and instruments in theatre”.

workedExamples.situation: A visitor asks to enter the main theatre while a case is in progress.
workedExamples.reasoning: The visitor changes into theatre clothing first, and scrubbed-staff rules apply close to the field. Keep the number of people moving in and out as low as possible (see “Movement, case order and cleaning between cases in the theatre”).

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves in the sizes and types the theatre plan lists, with spare pairs
Liquid-resistant mask plus goggles, or a face shield
Gown or plastic apron at the level the plan lists
Single-use caps and theatre shoes with waterproof soles

commonErrors.error: Wearing a theatre cap outside the theatre.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove the cap and dispose of it before leaving; never wear it outside.

commonErrors.error: Wearing open-front footwear in the theatre.
commonErrors.prevention: Choose snug shoes with waterproof soles, or galoshes.

commonErrors.error: Leaving a surgical mask around the neck when leaving the theatre.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove the mask before leaving the theatre.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Gloves are single-use and are never washed for reuse. Replace any damaged glove at once.
The four-level gown scale in the learner guide comes from a US standard and is not used.
Wedding ring rules differ between organisations. The theatre policy decides, and the learner guide rule applies where the organisation allows it.
Completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: Learner states the two jobs of gloves and when double gloving applies.
Learner names the headwear, footwear and jewellery rules without prompts.
Learner lists the items removed before leaving the theatre.
documentationEvidence: Checklist entry showing protective items were checked and fitted for the case.
Record of any glove change during a case, where the theatre keeps one.
summary: Gloves are single-use, and double gloving follows the theatre plan.
Headwear, footwear and jewellery rules protect the field and keep organisms out of it.
Mask and cap come off before leaving the theatre, and a white coat is worn in public areas.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why are scrubbed staff given disposable headwear in the theatre?
options: Because they work close to the surgical field, which matters most in laminar flow rooms
Because hair makes the theatre cap sit more comfortably and the cap is cooler to wear
To replace the need for hand hygiene and the gloves and gown are not needed
To show rank and seniority of each person in the theatre team and to mark the staff on the rota

knowledgeChecks.question: Which footwear is the better choice in theatre?
options: Open sandals with a thin sole, light and cool
Snug shoes with waterproof soles, or galoshes
Soft canvas slippers with a thin rubber sole
Bare feet with thin cotton socks on the floor

knowledgeChecks.question: What must happen to a surgical mask before a person leaves the theatre?
options: It is left tied around the neck after the case
It is taken off before the person leaves theatre
It is worn in the corridor for protection
It is passed to a visitor in the corridor

Conflict and resolution: the theatre document allows wedding rings for scrubbed and non-scrubbed staff; the learner guide permits a plain flat band only where the organisation allows. The learner guide governs the rule; the theatre policy decides.
UNCONFIRMED: AS 3789.6 (gown fabric) named in the theatre document. The four-level gown scale in the learner guide is from a US standard and is not used.

officialReferences.title: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (NHMRC, 2019)
officialReferences.pageDate: May 2019 (publication date shown in the document text; no web page date)
officialReferences.covers: The NHMRC guidelines say single-use, fit-for-purpose gloves are worn for invasive procedures, contact with sterile sites or non-intact skin or mucous membranes, and activities with a risk of exposure to blood or body substances; gloves are changed between patients; hand hygiene is performed before putting gloves on and after removing them; gowns are worn for a single procedure or episode of patient care where contamination is likely; and spills are confined and cleaned with absorbent material, then detergent solution. The text read does not address the gown fabric standard AS 3789.6.

officialReferences.title: AS 3789.6 (gown fabric standard, named in the operating-theatre source document)
officialReferences.covers: UNCONFIRMED (not confirmed by an official source): named in the source document only. The standard text, its current edition and any gown fabric requirement were not checked. Confirm on the Standards Australia catalogue before relying on any gown fabric point.
